title: Entrepreneurship, Economic Growth and Public Policy
abstract: This paper is an introduction to the second Global Entrepreneurship Research Conference. The conference focused on developing a better understanding of the relationships among entrepreneurship, economic growth and public policy, and variations according to the stage of economic development. The papers in this special issue conduct analysis with GEM micro-and-macro data, and offer several important policy recommendations. First, middle-income countries should focus on increasing human capital, upgrading technology availability and promoting enterprise development. It is important to start enterprise development policies early because the main drivers are perceptual variables that are difficult to change in the short run. Second, for developed economies, reducing entry regulations, in most cases, will not result in more high-potential startups. Both labor market reform and deregulation of financial markets may be needed to support growth of high-performance ventures.
summary_en: Ács and Szerb's introduction to the second Global Entrepreneurship Research Conference draws together cross-country evidence on the entrepreneurship-growth-policy relationship. They argue that the appropriate entrepreneurship policy depends on a country's stage of development. Middle-income countries (including Hungary) should focus on raising human capital, upgrading technology availability, and promoting enterprise development. Developed economies, by contrast, may not see more high-potential startups simply from reducing entry regulations — labour-market reform and financial-market deregulation may be needed.
data_used: Cross-country meta-review of papers in the Small Business Economics special issue (2007) using Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM) micro and macro data, covering 30+ countries at varying development stages.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungary's evolving entrepreneurship-policy framework. The paper supports the case that Hungary, as a middle-income economy, should prioritise human-capital and technology-upgrading investments over deregulation. Useful framing for ITM, Pénzügyminisztérium, and Hungarian academic institutions when designing the Hungarian National Smart Specialisation Strategy.
